placement.position_note: PARTY-LINE FRONTAGE, DERIVED FROM THE COMMITTED PLAT (T-0077). This building does not stand where a northing in the recipe put it: it stands on the north face of blk_lake_clark, whose line and bearing are read from the block boundary in data/traces/vectors/thompson_lots.json — the same committed geometry the lot grid and the corridor gate are derived from. Its front wall is set 0.80 m back from that lot line, the alignment the two frontage buildings already standing on this face use, and its east wall is fixed by the west wall of inf_butcher_market, which it shares a party line with. The bearing is the face's own, and this placement carries none of the jitter the parcel's interior rows carry, because a shared party wall is one wall and cannot wander. WHAT IS INVENTED IS STILL EVERYTHING THAT MATTERS: that a building stood here at all, which building it was, and that these particular units stood shoulder to shoulder. What the plate supports is the TREATMENT — a continuous storefront row on the town's principal street rather than detached cottages set back on grass — and the treatment is what this placement takes from it. Standing on a derived block face is not standing on a recovered lot.

It is NOT keyed to a construction season the way the named buildings' stocks are: this record's 1835-01-01 is the programme's count-unit convention and not a date anything was built, so keying to it would deal every anonymous roof in the town one stock. persons.name: James H. Phelps
persons.note: PROJECTED RESIDENT. Documented in Chicago post-office evidence but not independently corroborated strongly enough for attested circa-1835 residence. KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, IN ONE RETURN. The papers print 'Phelps, Jamea H.' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 20 May 1835, column 13 — dated 1835-05-20. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (docs/LIBERTIES.md L214), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py). No figure is drawn (L1). FERGUS 1839'S FORT DEARBORN ADDITION LOT SALE — JUNE 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. This person bid at the sale of the Fort Dearborn Addition, 10-24 June 1839, printed in Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 at pages 47-49. The bidder is printed as “J. J. Phelps”. 2 lot rows, $1,074 in all: block 8 lot 27 at $510 (f1839_lot0138, printed page 48); block 12 lot 5 at $564 (f1839_lot0220, printed page 49). The sale table's own shorthand, recorded and not flattened: 2 carry the block number forward from the last row that printed one. What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago between the 10th and the 24th of June 1839 and bid at the Fort Dearborn Addition sale. It is written as 1839 evidence with describes_date 1839-06, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected_resident, and a land sale four years after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. THE LOT IS NOT A LOCATION FOR 1835: the Fort Dearborn Addition is the Beaubien, or Reservation, lands, which in July 1835 were the garrison's ground and were not platted into lots at all. It places no house, no shop and no household in the town this project builds. No trade, no address in the town of 1835, no household and no house. The block and lot are the only location on the page, they are ground platted in 1839 out of the garrison's reservation, and they place nobody in the town of 1835. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Phelps' folds to the same string as the bidder's, and the given name of both begins J. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_lots_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a lot sale four years after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

persons.name: Aaron Russell
persons.note: A DOCUMENTED PERSON, AND NOTHING ELSE IS CLAIMED. The papers name 'Aapon Ruseell,' and 'Aaron Rusascll' and 'Aaron Russell' and give the trade; they do not say where this household lived, who else was in it, or when it came. So the record around this person carries nothing but the person: no dwelling, no division, no family, each written as unattested in its own block rather than filled in from the shape of the rest of the town. Cited at the Democrat of 29 October 1834, column 6; the Democrat of 12 November 1834, column 11; the Democrat of 3 September 1834, column 12. The corpus associates the name with Water Street; that is where the paper does business with this person and not a statement about where they slept, and the storefront tickets are the ones that may stand a shop there. THE TOWN NEVER INVENTED A ROOF FOR THIS TRADE. The occupation census raised reconstructed households for the trades a town of 3,265 people needed and could not document; `bookseller` was not one of them, which is why this person could only ever be ADDED and never seated on an existing record — data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json calls it `new_resident` for exactly that reason. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1). READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, not a scan: the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 grades a transcription-mediated reading as documented, and the source record for the run states that standard and its limits. A scan read that confirms or corrects the name upgrades this entry.

residents.research_note: MINTED FROM THE NEWSPAPER REGISTER (T-0376), AND THE HOUSEHOLD IS A CONTAINER RATHER THAN AN ARGUMENT. Every other record in this dataset argues for a household — a family the sources count, or a trade the town demonstrably needed. This one argues for a PERSON: the Democrat and the American name Aaron Russell as a bookseller at Chicago 3 time(s), and this reconstruction did not hold them. `data/residents/` has no way to carry a person except inside a household, so one was written around them and told to claim nothing: one member, no dwelling, no division, no origin, no arrival beyond the bound the paper sets. Reading a family, a house or a quarter of town into this record would be reading something the papers do not say. tools/mint_documented_residents.py derives the whole minted set and prints every candidate it refused, with the reason.

what_it_supplies: A 665-roof production target with independently reconcilable group, district, level, and construction totals.
Thirty-five architectural family definitions with dimensional and massing bands.
District character, spacing, variation, finish, and chronology constraints for a July 1835 reconstruction.
A required distinction between named documentary landmarks and anonymous inferred infill.
what_it_does_not_supply: A surviving July 1835 building census or parcel-by-parcel roof register.
Exact locations, dimensions, appearance, occupants, or construction dates for anonymous roofs.
Authority to replace stronger building-specific evidence already represented in the dataset.

fabric_basis.words: whitewashed clapboard on a balloon frame, 12-over-12 sash of 6 × 8 in glass, plain corner boards and a stoop, under a weathered roof — a one-room frame cottage, a year old (rule F-T: a tradesman's by its type)

frontage.why: T-0077, the owner's ask of 2026-08-18 on the Tremont House street scene: "there should be more and denser buildings. this is important." He sent the plate of this corner — a continuous two-storey storefront row, shoulder to shoulder on shared party lines — beside a screenshot of this same corner in the render, where the Tremont stands alone on open grass. Four of this row's anonymous roofs stood in the Clark-Dearborn block SEVENTEEN TO TWENTY-FOUR METRES behind the Lake Street frontage, each nudged off the line by its own jitter, which is the shape of a distribution and not of a street. They now stand ON the frontage: the line, its bearing and the corner they pack back from are read from the committed block boundary in data/traces/vectors/thompson_lots.json, and this file authors no coordinate for any of them. The 0.80 m setback is not a measurement — it is the line the two frontage buildings ALREADY standing on this face (inf_bakery_lake and inf_butcher_market) use, adopted so the street wall is one wall rather than three. No roof is added, moved out of its block, renamed or re-dimensioned: the parcel still deals 40 principal and 8 ancillary, and every id and band is the one it was.
